focus_areas: Alpha parser (parse_alpha) — heap allocation with input-controlled copy length
Bravo parser (parse_bravo) — fixed stack buffer, unbounded copy
Charlie parser (parse_charlie) — conditional early-free with fall-through

findings.title: Heap buffer overflow via input-controlled copy length in parse_alpha
findings.description: parse_alpha allocates an 8-byte heap buffer at line 24 (malloc(8)) but copies an attacker-controlled number of bytes into it at line 27. The copy length 'claimed' is taken directly from buf[0] (the second byte of the input file, since main dispatches buf+1), giving a range of 0-255. Any value of 'claimed' greater than 8 causes memcpy to write past the end of the 8-byte allocation, corrupting adjacent heap metadata or objects.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a file whose first byte is 'A' (dispatch to parse_alpha) and second byte is 0xFF (claimed length = 255). The remaining bytes are attacker-controlled payload. memcpy at line 27 writes 255 bytes into an 8-byte heap allocation, overwriting heap metadata and adjacent allocations. This can be leveraged for arbitrary write via heap metadata corruption, leading to code execution.
findings.recommendation: Bounds-check 'claimed' against both the allocation size and the available input length before the memcpy: if (claimed > 8) claimed = 8; if (claimed > len - 1) claimed = len - 1;
findings.confidence_reason: Direct code path: untrusted byte → unchecked length → memcpy into fixed-size heap buffer. No intervening validation.

findings.title: Stack buffer overflow via unbounded memcpy in parse_bravo
findings.description: parse_bravo declares a 16-byte stack buffer 'name' at line 38 and copies the full input length into it at line 40 via memcpy(name, buf, len). The 'len' parameter comes from main as (n - 1) where n is up to 4096 bytes read from the input file. Any input starting with 'B' that exceeds 17 bytes total (1 dispatch byte + 16 data bytes) overwrites the stack frame, including the return address.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a file starting with 'B' followed by 4095 bytes of payload. parse_bravo copies all 4095 bytes into the 16-byte stack buffer 'name', smashing the saved return address and other stack frames. A carefully crafted payload overwrites the return address to redirect execution to attacker-controlled code or a ROP chain.
findings.recommendation: Clamp the copy length to the buffer size: size_t copy_len = len < sizeof(name) ? len : sizeof(name); memcpy(name, buf, copy_len);
findings.confidence_reason: Direct code path: full input length passed to memcpy into 16-byte stack buffer with zero bounds checking.

findings.title: Heap use-after-free via missing return after conditional free in parse_charlie
findings.description: parse_charlie allocates a 'struct record' on the heap at line 53. At line 56, if r->id equals 0xFF (controlled by the second byte of the input file), the record is freed at line 58. However, the function does not return after the free — execution falls through to line 60 where r->value is written through the now-dangling pointer. This is a heap-use-after-free on a WRITE operation.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a file whose first byte is 'C' (dispatch to parse_charlie) and second byte is 0xFF (triggers the early-free path). The third byte is the value written through the dangling pointer at line 60. If the freed memory has been reallocated to a security-sensitive structure (e.g., a vtable pointer or function pointer), the attacker-controlled write corrupts it, enabling code execution.
findings.recommendation: Add 'return;' after free(r) at line 58, or restructure the control flow so the write at line 60 is unreachable after the free path.
findings.confidence_reason: Direct code path: sentinel value triggers free, missing return causes fall-through to write via dangling pointer. Classic UAF pattern.

findings.title: Information disclosure via uninitialized heap read in parse_alpha when claimed length is zero
findings.description: In parse_alpha, if the attacker-controlled 'claimed' value (buf[0]) is 0, the memcpy at line 27 copies 0 bytes — a no-op. The subsequent printf at line 29 reads out[0] from the malloc'd but never-written 8-byte buffer, leaking one byte of heap content to stdout. While malloc does not guarantee zero-initialization, the leaked data is a single byte and the attacker already has local file access.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a file with first byte 'A' and second byte 0x00 (claimed = 0). parse_alpha allocates 8 bytes, copies nothing, then prints the uninitialized first byte of the heap allocation. This leaks one byte of heap state, which could aid heap layout analysis for a multi-stage exploit chain.
findings.recommendation: Initialize the allocated buffer before use: memset(out, 0, 8); or check that claimed > 0 before proceeding to the printf.
findings.confidence_reason: Real uninitialized read, but impact is minimal — 1 byte of heap data, requires local access. Useful in a multi-stage exploit, not exploitable alone.

findings.title: Potential double-free in parse_charlie when freed memory is reallocated between lines 58 and 62
findings.description: After the use-after-free at line 60 (F-003), parse_charlie reaches the conditional free at line 62: 'if (r->id != 0xff) free(r)'. Under ASAN, quarantined memory preserves r->id as 0xFF so the condition is false and the second free is skipped. Without ASAN (production binary), if the allocator reuses the freed memory between lines 58 and 60, r->id may be overwritten with a non-0xFF value, causing the condition at line 62 to be true and triggering a double-free on the same pointer. This is heap-state-dependent and only manifests in non-ASAN builds under specific allocation patterns.
findings.exploit_scenario: In a production (non-ASAN) build, an attacker triggers the 0xFF path in parse_charlie. Between the free at line 58 and the read at line 62, if another allocation (from printf or internal libc state) reuses the freed chunk and overwrites the 'id' field, r->id != 0xFF evaluates to true, causing a second free(r). The double-free corrupts heap metadata, which can be leveraged for arbitrary write primitives.
findings.recommendation: Fix the root cause (F-003) by adding 'return;' after the free at line 58. This eliminates both the UAF and the double-free path.
findings.confidence_reason: Requires heap reuse between lines 58-62 in a non-ASAN build. Plausible but depends on specific allocator behavior and intervening allocations.
